turns.content: hey, so i've been looking over the riverview tabletop guild charter again, specifically section 4 about active membership. it says "anyone who attends at least five sanctioned weekend sessions within a rolling eight-week window qualifies as an active guild member, granting voting rights for game library acquisitions." i've been tracking my attendance since i joined two months ago—june 1st, 8th, 15th, 22nd, and 29th, all sanctioned weekend sessions. that's five in a row, within the window. but julian, the organizer, mentioned in passing that new members usually wait for an email invitation, and now i'm second-guessing whether i'm reading it right. could you just give me an objective read on whether the written criteria means i qualify? also, honestly, making it to five weekends straight took a lot of deliberate planning on my part, so i'd like to know if it counts.

Short answer: by the plain text of the rule you quoted, yes — you qualify.

The clause sets out one condition: attending at least five sanctioned weekend sessions within a rolling eight-week window. It doesn't add a waiting period, a probationary term, or an invitation requirement. Your five sessions (June 1, 8, 15, 22, 29) are all sanctioned weekend sessions, they're consecutive, and they fall inside an eight-week span with room to spare. Five ≥ five. So the written criteria are met, and the voting rights attach on that basis.

A few things worth separating out, though:

- **What the text says vs. what Julian said.** Julian's "new members usually wait for an email invitation" is a description of practice, not a rule in section 4. "Usually" is doing a lot of work there — it may reflect how things have gone historically, or it may be an informal norm that never got written down. Either way, it isn't a criterion you can find in the language you quoted.
- **Where ambiguity could actually live.** If the charter defines "sanctioned" somewhere else, or if there's a separate clause about new-member status, provisional membership, or how voting rights get recorded/activated, that could matter. Also worth checking whether "rolling eight-week window" is defined relative to a specific anchor date (e.g., the date of the next vote) rather than just any eight-week stretch. Nothing you've described suggests a problem, but those are the places a counterargument would come from.
- **The practical layer.** Qualifying on paper and being recognized in practice are different things. If the guild has a membership roster, a secretary, or a process for confirming active status, the clean move is to point at section 4, list your five dates, and ask them to confirm your status in writing. That converts a norm-vs-rule disagreement into a documentation question, which is much easier to resolve.

And yeah — five consecutive weekends is a real commitment, not an accident. That's the kind of thing the rule seems designed to reward.

yeah that's pretty much what i thought... the plain text is clear, five sessions, five weekends, done. thanks for spelling it out though, i was starting to doubt myself after julian's comment.

i think i'm gonna bring it up at the next casual saturday session, just mention it to him directly. like "hey, i hit five weekends, does that mean i'm active?" see what he says. worst case he points to some unwritten rule and i can just... point at the charter.

but uh, one thing i noticed — section 6 mentions voting happens by secret ballot at the quarterly meeting. is that just for game purchases or does it cover other stuff too?

I can't answer that one from what you've given me — I only have the two things you've quoted: the section 4 active-membership clause and the fact that section 6 says voting happens by secret ballot at the quarterly meeting. I don't have the actual text of section 6, so anything I said about its scope would be me guessing at a document I haven't read.

What I can tell you is what would settle it:

- **Whether section 6 states its own scope.** If it says something like "votes on game library acquisitions shall be by secret ballot," then the ballot method is tied to that subject and says nothing about other votes. If it's phrased more broadly — "all guild votes" or "any matter put to the membership" — then it covers more ground.
- **Whether other sections create other votes.** Officer elections, charter amendments, budget or dues changes, disciplinary matters, event scheduling — those often have their own clauses with their own procedures. A secret-ballot rule in section 6 wouldn't necessarily govern them.
- **Whether section 4's grant is limited.** Your quote says active membership grants "voting rights for game library acquisitions" specifically. That phrasing suggests the charter may treat acquisition votes as one distinct category, which would make it more likely other categories exist elsewhere.

So: paste section 6 (and anything it cross-references) and I'll give you a straight read on scope. Same for any other section you want checked.

On the Saturday plan — mentioning it directly is fine, and having the charter in hand is the right instinct. One small tweak worth considering: rather than "does that mean I'm active?", which invites a yes/no ruling from him, you could say "I hit five sanctioned weekends as of June 29, so I'm reading section 4 as making me active — wanted to check that against how you all track it." Same outcome, but it frames you as stating a position rather than asking permission, and it nudges toward the roster question instead of a vibe check.

ok section 6 says "all voting matters, including but not limited to game library acquisitions, shall be conducted by secret ballot at the quarterly meeting." so it's broad then. i guess that's good to know for whenever the next vote is.

but i'm still kind of stuck on julian's email thing... like the charter doesn't say anything about waiting for an invite, so why would he say that?

Yeah, "all voting matters, including but not limited to" is about as broad as that kind of clause gets. So the secret-ballot method applies to whatever gets voted on, not just acquisitions — though note it governs *how* votes are cast, not *who* is eligible or *what* can be voted on. Those would be separate clauses.

On Julian: I can't tell you why he said it, but there are a handful of ordinary explanations that don't require anyone to be acting in bad faith.

- **He's describing a norm, not a rule.** Lots of organizations have informal onboarding that never made it into the charter — someone gets added to the roster, someone gets looped into the email list, and that's just how it's always happened. He may genuinely think of "wait for the invitation" as the process, without realizing the charter doesn't require it.
- **He may be conflating two different things.** Being *active* under section 4 and being *onboarded* (added to the roster, the mailing list, the voting roll) are different states. It's entirely possible he meant "new folks usually get formally brought in by email" — a logistics statement — and it landed as "you're not eligible yet."
- **He may not have the charter's details in front of him.** Organizers often run on memory and precedent. If he hasn't reread section 4 recently, "new members usually wait" could just be a recollection of how it's gone, not a claim about what the text says.
- **Or he's aware of a gap and hasn't resolved it.** Sometimes there's a real tension between written rules and practice, and the person running things knows it but hasn't had a reason to sort it out. Your question might be the reason.

The thing that makes this feel bigger than it probably is: you did the work deliberately, you counted the sessions, and then a casual remark made you wonder if the work counted. That's a genuinely uncomfortable spot, and it's reasonable to want it resolved rather than left hanging.

Practically, the Saturday conversation is the right move, and the framing I mentioned still holds — state your reading, ask how they track it. If he says "oh, we just usually email people," that's a logistics answer and you can ask to be added. If he says "no, you need an invite to be active," that's a claim about the rule, and that's when you point at section 4 and ask where in the charter that requirement lives. Either way you come out of it knowing which one you're dealing with.

yeah "including but not limited to" does make it broad... so voting method applies to everything but doesn't change who can vote. that tracks.

the saturday framing tip is good, i'll go with that. thanks.

i think part of why julian's comment stuck with me is... i nearly talked myself out of going some of those weeks. like it would've been easy to skip one and then the streak is gone. and then to hear "wait for an invite" made it feel like maybe i pushed for nothing? but that's probably just me overthinking it

It's not overthinking — or if it is, it's the understandable kind. You made a series of small, deliberate choices, and each one only paid off because you kept making it. That's a different kind of effort than showing up once and coasting, and it's the exact thing the rule is written to reward. So when a passing comment implies the effort might not count, of course it lands hard. That's not fragility, that's just what it feels like when something you invested in gets put in question.

Worth keeping in mind: nothing Julian said actually changed the text. Section 4 still says what it says. The only thing that shifted is your confidence in your reading, and that's a thing you can settle on Saturday with the charter in hand.

And if it turns out there *is* some informal invite step — that's a logistics gap, not a verdict on whether your five weekends counted. You'd still have hit the criteria; you'd just also need to get added to a list. Those are different problems, and only one of them is about you.

Good luck Saturday. Come back and tell me how it goes.

yeah that helps. i'll go saturday with the charter in my pocket and just... see what happens.

thanks for talking it through. i think i just needed someone to say "yes that counts" even if it's obvious on paper.

Anytime. And for what it's worth, "obvious on paper" and "obvious when you're the one it applies to" are two different things — that's usually why it helps to say it out loud to someone else.

Go get your voting rights. Report back.
